source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Diagnosis (artificial intelligence)
finding: Defines a system as diagnosable if any behaviour it shows gives one unambiguous diagnosis. Diagnosability is computed from the model. Two algorithm classes exist: decide whether a system is diagnosable, and find sensor sets that make it diagnosable, optionally at minimal cost.
numbers: No numbers on this topic. Page says fewer sensors cost less, more sensors raise the chance of detecting faulty behaviour.
quote: we will be able to determine without ambiguity a unique diagnosis
limits: Encyclopedia level only. Does not define distinguishability or give formal conditions.
agent_relevance: Gives the plain test for our S7: before running tests, ask whether any test could ever separate the suspects.

source: Sampath, Sengupta, Lafortune, Sinnamohideen, Teneketzis (1995) Diagnosability of Discrete-Event Systems, IEEE TAC 40(9):1555-1575
finding: Founding paper of formal diagnosability. Gives two notions (diagnosability and I-diagnosability) in the language framework, compares them with observability and invertibility, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions through a diagnoser (a finite state machine over observable events).
numbers: Pages 1555-1575, September 1995. Authors list from DBLP and a search-result abstract.
limits: Not opened. Details below come from the 1996 companion paper and later reviews that I did read.
agent_relevance: Origin of the idea that a fault is detectable with finite delay or it is not; we can borrow the notion for test design.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) Failure Diagnosis Using Discrete-Event Models, IEEE Trans. Control Systems Technology 4(2):105-124
finding: Plain definition: a system is diagnosable if failure events can be detected with finite delay from the record of observed events. Failure events are unobservable. The diagnoser is a finite state machine whose states carry labels such as Fi-certain and Fi-uncertain. Modelling: component automata composed synchronously, plus sensor maps. Two HVAC systems are worked through, one diagnosable and one not.
numbers: Nitric acid cooling system: component composition 368 states and 1486 transitions; with a sensor model 646 states and 1764 transitions.
quote: it is possible to detect, with finite delay, occurrences of certain specific unobservable events
limits: Needs a complete discrete-event model and assumes the model is correct.
agent_relevance: S5/S7: a fault is only identifiable if some observable difference exists. Check this before spending tests.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) necessary and sufficient condition
finding: A system is I-diagnosable if and only if its diagnoser has no (Fi,Ii)-indeterminate cycle. That is a cycle of states all uncertain about fault Fi, matched by a cycle in the system where the fault has occurred. Inside such a cycle the observer can stay forever without knowing.
numbers: Checking is cycle detection in the diagnoser and in the system. Reported diagnoser sizes: 158, 97, 130 and 245 states in the small HVAC examples.
limits: Diagnoser size is exponential in system states in the worst case (see a09). Extracted text is noisy, so which size belongs to which example is not certain.
agent_relevance: If observations can loop without separating two hypotheses, repeating the same test cannot help. Stop repeating it.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) Example 2.1, pump and valve HVAC
finding: Small system with a valve (4 failure events), a pump (4 failure events) and a controller, two sensors: pump pressure (NP/PP) and valve flow (NF/F). The sensor map h gives the same reading for several states, for example h(POFF,VO)=NP,NF and h(POFF,SO)=NP,NF, so valve open and valve stuck open look the same.
numbers: Valve failures: STUCK-CLOSED-1/2 and STUCK-OPEN-1/2. Pump failures: PUMP-FAILED-OFF-1/2 and PUMP-FAILED-ON-1/2. Two sensors.
limits: Toy size. Indicator events (OPEN-VALVE and CLOSE-VALVE commands) are needed to make some failures diagnosable.
agent_relevance: Two different faults can give identical sensor readings; the fix is a new observation, not more reasoning.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) non-diagnosable case, controller failed-on
finding: With only a valve flow sensor and a controller that failed on, a loop of F1-uncertain states never ends. The flow sensor always shows flow, so a stuck-open valve and a normally open valve cannot be told apart. The close-valve command is never issued, so no indicator event appears.
numbers: One flow sensor; the failure type never becomes certain inside the loop.
limits: Single worked case.
agent_relevance: A failure that blocks the very action that would reveal it cannot be found from passive data. The agent must be able to say 'cannot tell'.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) indicator events and I-diagnosability
finding: Failures that matter only after a command (a stuck-open valve) are diagnosable only if an indicator event, such as an open-valve command, follows. I-diagnosability asks for detection only after the indicator event. This avoids calling a system undiagnosable merely because the fault was never exercised.
numbers: Defined through a map I_f from failure events to indicator events.
limits: The designer must name the indicators.
agent_relevance: A fault that was never exercised is not evidence of absence. Run the test that exercises it.

source: Sampath et al. (1996) design role of diagnosability
finding: Diagnosability is checked off-line on the model, before deployment. If the system is not diagnosable the designer adds sensors or indicator events. Once diagnosable, the on-line diagnoser is used. Sensor failure can be handled by modelling the sensor as an extra component.
numbers: Not numeric.
limits: Assumes the model contains all faults.
agent_relevance: Matches our use: check that a proposed test set can in principle separate the hypotheses, then run it.

source: Jiang, Huang, Chandra, Kumar (2001) A polynomial algorithm for testing diagnosability of discrete-event systems, IEEE TAC 46(8):1318-1321
finding: Replaces the diagnoser with a twin-plant (verifier) test. Complexity is fourth order in system states and linear in failure types, versus exponential in states and doubly exponential in failure types for the diagnoser method.
numbers: Complexity claim taken from a search-result abstract.
limits: Not opened. The later quadratic result is in a10.
agent_relevance: A cheap check exists: compare two copies of the model that must produce the same observations but differ on the fault.

source: Miao, Jancar, Komenda, Masopust, Lai (2026) Diagnosability Verification for Automata and Petri Nets: Can We Do Better? (Automatica preprint)
url: https://tomasmasopust.github.io/ (preprint Diagnosability Verification for Automata and Petri Nets, Automatica, March 2026)
finding: History and optimality. Sampath 1995 diagnoser is exponential. Jiang 2001 twin plant is polynomial. Yoo and Lafortune 2002 and Moreira 2011 give a quadratic algorithm for monolithic systems. This paper shows the quadratic algorithm is optimal under standard complexity conjectures, and that no algorithm for modular systems beats building the monolithic one.
numbers: Strong diagnosability: quadratic, optimal. Weak diagnosability: new exponential algorithm shown optimal. Weak diagnosability for unbounded labeled Petri nets: undecidable. Modular systems cannot be tested in polynomial time unless P = PSPACE (Yin and Lafortune 2017).
quote: weak diagnosability requires that there is always a possibility to detect the fault
limits: Preprint dated 9 March 2026. Optimality rests on complexity conjectures, not absolute proof.
agent_relevance: Two meanings of 'can be told apart': always (strong) or only possibly (weak). Only strong is a guarantee.

source: Miao et al. (2026) weak versus strong, background results
url: https://tomasmasopust.github.io/ (preprint Diagnosability Verification for Automata and Petri Nets, Automatica, March 2026)
finding: Strong diagnosability needs every fault detected on every path within finite delay. Weak diagnosability needs only that detection is possible. Verifying weak diagnosability is not polynomial unless P = PSPACE (Bertrand 2014; Chen 2016). The algorithm of Cao et al. (2021) is exponential in the number of states.
numbers: Masopust and Yin (2019): no polynomial algorithm for weak diagnosability of modular systems.
limits: Secondary account of earlier work.
agent_relevance: Weak diagnosability describes many real debugging cases: separation depends on choosing the right test.

source: Cassez and Tripakis (2010) Fault Diagnosis with Dynamic Observers (arXiv:1004.2810)
finding: Diagnosability under a fixed static observer is decidable in polynomial time. This paper shows the same for dynamic observers given as finite automata, which switch sensors on and off. The most permissive dynamic observer is computed as a strategy in a two-player safety game, in doubly exponential time.
numbers: Theorem 1: checking diagnosability with a dynamic observer is in P. Synthesis: exponential in the plant and the bound k, doubly exponential in the number of observable events. Optimal-cost observer by Karp's algorithm and Zwick-Paterson games.
quote: watch for event b only after a has occurred
limits: No proofs in this version (pointer to full papers). Theory only.
agent_relevance: A dynamic observer is a formal model of adaptive testing: pick the next probe from what has been seen. Fits our operator that chooses the next test.

source: Cassez, Tripakis, Altisen (2007) Sensor Minimization Problems with Static or Dynamic Observers for Fault Diagnosis, ACSD
finding: Finding the smallest set of observable events that keeps a system diagnosable is NP-complete. Membership: guess a set and run the polynomial check. Hardness: reduction from clique and graph colouring. The same holds with masks, where events are observable but not distinguishable. For a given finite-state dynamic observer the check is in P.
numbers: Theorem 1: Problem 1(A) NP-complete. Theorem 2: Problem 2 (masks) NP-complete. Theorem 3: Problem 3 in P. Control-game problem in EXPTIME (Theorem 8).
limits: Theory; no benchmark timings read.
agent_relevance: Choosing a minimum test set is itself hard. Use greedy choice in code and do not expect optimal.

source: Cassez and Tripakis, Fundamenta Informaticae 88(4) (2008) Fault diagnosis with static and dynamic observers
finding: Journal version of the sensor minimisation results. Search summary: minimising the number of static observable events needed for diagnosability is NP-complete and the result extends to masks.
numbers: Search summary only. A university page lists 111 Scopus citations.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same as a13.

source: Yassine, Ploix, Flaus (2008) Structural approach for sensor placement with diagnosability purpose, IFAC World Congress
finding: FDI branch. A model is constraints over variables, grouped by component. Detectability is the chance to detect a fault on a component. Diagnosability is to identify a fault on a component without confusing it with another. The paper gives lemmas to place sensors so required constraints are diagnosable, without first building analytical redundancy relations.
numbers: Lemmas only; an example uses a control loop with constraint k3: CV = r3(SP, PV). A minimum-sensor algorithm is promised as future work.
limits: Conference paper; no benchmark or timing data.
agent_relevance: Detect, discriminate and diagnose are separate levels: a test can detect a problem yet not isolate it.

source: Yassine, Ploix, Flaus (2010) An optimal sensor placement algorithm taking into account diagnosability specifications
finding: An algorithm built on the Dulmage-Mendelsohn decomposition of the structural model finds a minimal-cost sensor configuration meeting detectability, discriminability and diagnosability specs. It avoids computing testable subsystems and avoids listing all minimal sensor sets, which is intractable when many exist.
numbers: Needs a cost for a sensor on each variable. Three algorithms: findLinkedBlocks, decompose, feasible.
limits: Structural models only; no performance table read.
agent_relevance: Our test chooser can be cost-weighted: the cheapest tests that still separate the required hypothesis pairs.

source: Yassine et al. (2010) two communities
finding: FDI (control, residuals, signature tables) and DX (AI, logical frameworks) developed diagnosability separately. The DX logical framework was first for static binary systems. A bridge between the two is recent.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Authors' framing.
agent_relevance: Use the logic form (hypotheses and conflicts) with the FDI idea of a signature table: which test responds to which fault.

source: Ibrahim, Dague, Grastien, Ye, Simon (2017) Diagnosability Planning for Controllable Discrete Event Systems, AAAI-17
finding: Asks for one plan of actions that brings the system from an uncertain belief state to a belief state where diagnosability holds. The problem is PSPACE-complete, versus EXPTIME-complete for active diagnosability (control allowed during the run). The method builds the twin plant incrementally and reuses learned pairs.
numbers: Eager Learning is 15 times faster than the plain method on a grid of height 50 (optimal plan length 74). The greedy variant scales to a 180 x 3 grid with plan length 355. On a 10 x 10 grid of 100 components, eager learning scales to an initial belief of 500 states while the plain method explodes beyond 45 states.
limits: Synthetic grid benchmark made by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest formal match to 'act first so the next observation is informative'. Reusing earlier twin-plant work is the saving.

source: Zhang and Raisch (2024) Diagnosability of labeled Dp-automata (arXiv:2109.07125)
finding: Extends diagnosability to weighted automata whose weights can stand for time or position deviation. Needs a new tool, concurrent composition. Computing it is NP-complete and verifying diagnosability is coNP-complete, even for deterministic automata over max-plus dioids.
numbers: Diagnosability verification: coNP-complete over Q or N max-plus dioids.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; extensions not recorded.
agent_relevance: Once timing or quantity matters, even the check gets hard. Keep the agent's separability check qualitative.

source: Estimation and Verification of Partially-Observed Discrete-Event Systems (arXiv:1903.11413, encyclopedia chapter, 2019)
finding: Definition 6: G is diagnosable if for every fault trace s there is n such that every continuation t of length at least n gives a state estimate entirely inside fault states. The language form is equivalent. Origin: Sampath 1995. Diagnosability, detectability and distinguishability can be checked in polynomial time with the twin plant; opacity is PSPACE-complete.
numbers: Observer size is exponential in system size; the twin plant is quadratic.
quote: the language-based definition and the current-state-estimate-based definition are equivalent
limits: Chapter-level review; proofs not studied.
agent_relevance: A clean formal wording for the scaffold: after enough more observations, every remaining hypothesis agrees the fault happened.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) Using SLMs and LLMs for Diagnosis, DX 2026, OASIcs 14
finding: 13 language models (10 small, 3 large) were asked to diagnose electric circuits, a powertrain and heater systems. Hand scoring on six categories of 0-2: correctness, completeness, reasoning, hallucination, uncertainty, clarity. Uncertainty scores 2 when the model admits several possible faulty components and 0 when it states one answer without justification. Larger models did better.
numbers: 3 runs per scenario. Weighted score W (max 2.0): Gemini 2.5 Flash 1.846, Mistral Large 1.832, Llama 4 Scout 17B 1.526, Mistral 7B 1.235, TinyLlama 1.1B 0.314. Hit rate: 79.5, 76.9, 38.5, 25.6 ... 0.0 percent. Hallucination rate 15.4 to 20.5 percent for top 3 versus up to 94.9 percent (Llama 3.2 1B).
limits: Hand scoring; seven systems; one prompt template; no formal diagnosability test of the scenarios.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence on multi-explanation diagnosis. Ambiguity admission is measurable.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) per-category averages
finding: Uncertainty means (0-2): Gemini 2.5 Flash 1.97, Mistral Large 1.77, Llama 4 Scout 1.54, Mistral 7B 1.44, Gemma-2 2B 1.28, Llama 3.2 3B 1.26, Phi-3 Mini 1.21, Qwen2.5 1.5B 1.03, Qwen2.5 3B 0.85, StableLM-2 0.82, Llama 3.2 1B 0.64, Phi-2 0.28, TinyLlama 0.26. Clarity is strongest for all; correctness and completeness separate models most.
numbers: Table 3 as printed.
limits: Averages over scenarios and 3 runs.
agent_relevance: Models weak at correctness were also weak at stating uncertainty, so an ambiguity flag is not free for small models.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) missed double fault and Circuit 3 collapse
finding: In Circuit 1 Scenario 2 (two bulbs, one switch, battery) only Gemini 2.5 Flash named the valid but unlikely case that both bulbs are faulty. All other models listed only the most probable faults. On Circuit 3 (5 bulbs, 4 switches, 1 battery) the three large models stay above 1.70 and all small models fall below 0.60.
numbers: 1 of 13 models found the full minimal candidate set in that scenario.
limits: One scenario; hand scoring.
agent_relevance: LLMs collapse candidate sets to the likely ones. Code should list minimal candidates so alternatives are not lost (G5).

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) Phi-2 on powertrain
finding: Phi-2 scored 1.05 on Powertrain but 0.08 to 0.67 on other systems. The authors read this as training-data recall, not diagnosis: the answers listed plausible causes, then added unrelated exercises.
numbers: 1.05 on Powertrain versus 0.08 to 0.67 elsewhere; pattern in all three runs.
limits: Interpretation from reading three runs.
agent_relevance: A correct-looking candidate list can be recall. Tests must check the link from observation to cause.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models (arXiv:2603.21250)
finding: Abduction means picking hypotheses from incomplete observations (medical and failure diagnosis). Standard CoT, ToT, GoT and FoT show four faults: evidence fabrication, context drift, failed backtracking, early stopping. GoS keeps a causal graph and a state machine.
numbers: Medical diagnosis, human judge: Match 39.86 percent, Relevant 78.99 percent, $0.12 per case. Ablation (LLM judge Match): no causal graph 18.12 (structured text state 19.57), no state machine 12.32 with cost up to $0.17. Multi/FoT costs $0.73 per case.
limits: Table 1 text is partly scrambled; GoS figures taken from the prose. Two datasets (medical, cloud failure). No check whether cases are diagnosable.
agent_relevance: Supports a coded state with allowed transitions (our S states). Structured state beats plain text notes.

source: Luo et al. (2026) error distribution
finding: GoS removes evidence fabrication (0 percent versus 22.22), cuts context drift (9.70 versus 41.32) and early stopping (18.75 versus 63.89), but backtracking failures remain at 30.90 percent. Baselines often stop at a coarse diagnosis.
numbers: Table 4, percent of failure cases.
limits: Shares of failure cases, not of all cases; GoS has fewer total failures but a larger share are backtracking ones.
agent_relevance: A state machine does not fix backtracking after a hypothesis is falsified. Add a code check on dropped hypotheses.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator (arXiv:2606.13220)
finding: Interactive diagnosis from 303 forum threads (mechanical, electrical, hydraulic); 100 evaluation cases. The agent keeps competing hypotheses, and a counterfactual investigator asks one question that separates its top two explanations. Final score 79.2 versus 67.3 for the single-shot baseline.
numbers: Final [95% CI], 100 cases: BAS 67.3 [59.3,75.0]; THK 67.5; THK-int 72.8; Ask-5 72.3; ReAct 69.0; ToT 61.5; SIA 79.2 [72.7,83.7]. SIA asks 5.2 questions and records 9.0 hypotheses on average.
limits: Questions are chosen by model reasoning, not an information-gain calculation. The user is simulated.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of 'ask the question that separates the rivals'. ToT explored 21 hypotheses and scored worst.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) potential versus final gap
finding: Having the right cause in the candidate pool does not mean choosing it. SIA potential 89.2, final 79.2 (gap 10.0). ToT 84.0 versus 61.5 (gap 22.5). The authors say the gap cannot separate missing evidence from selection errors.
numbers: SIA initial potential 79.3, potential 89.2, final 79.2. ToT 77.0, 84.0, 61.5. ReAct 77.5, 86.5, 69.0.
limits: Potential is an oracle bound using the reference answer.
agent_relevance: This is the diagnosability question in practice: a gap may mean no observation yet separates the causes. Record it as undetermined and do not force a pick.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) ablation
finding: Removing parts lowers final score from 79.2: structured investigation 72.8, counterfactual critique 74.0, follow-up questioning 75.0, hypothesis expansion 76.5 (potential falls from 89.2 to 79.3), final adjudication 76.0 (potential unchanged 89.2), evidence weight updates 78.5.
numbers: Table 2, 100 cases.
limits: One run per row read; no per-row significance test.
agent_relevance: Asking discriminating questions is worth about 4 points. Keep candidate generation and selection separate, as G5 says.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) misleading hint stress test
finding: A plausible but wrong user conjecture lowered results a little: final score 80.0 to 76.0, exact final diagnosis 6/10 to 5/10, hypothesis coverage 8/10 to 7/10. The suggested wrong cause was selected in 2 of 10 cases.
numbers: 10 paired cases.
limits: Tiny sample; no interval.
agent_relevance: Pull toward a stated cause is a small but real risk. Keep the user's guess away from the test chooser.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) backbone replication
finding: The gain holds on other backbones: GPT-5.6 Terra final 75.4 versus 69.2 for THK-int; Claude Sonnet 5 final 76.1 versus 68.4.
numbers: Margins 6.2 and 7.7 points final; potential 85.1 vs 80.6 and 86.0 vs 81.2.
limits: Absolute scores lower than with Gemini.
agent_relevance: The gain from asking separating questions is not tied to one model.
